Subject: Checking in after this morning

Hi Naveen,

I wanted to write properly, because at the stand-up I only managed a clumsy "you okay?"

When the director started going through the quarterly numbers, your face went grey and your hands were shaking so much the coffee cup rattled on the table. My first thought, honestly, was that you were scared of the review. I nearly said "relax, it's not that bad."

I'm glad I asked instead whether you'd eaten. When you said nothing since last night, I got the juice from the pantry and sat with you in the small room until your hands stopped trembling.

You said afterwards it was "probably both, the hunger and the nerves." Fair enough. I just didn't want to guess at the feeling before checking you were physically all right. If it keeps happening, please get it checked with a doctor.

Hafsa

qa.a: Hafsa got the juice from the pantry and sat with Naveen in the small room until the trembling stopped.

qa.a: Asking whether Naveen had eaten and staying with Naveen worked, because it dealt with a possible physical cause before anyone judged the mood.

qa.a: Naveen might have felt misread and embarrassed, since part of the shaking came from not eating, and would still have been unwell.

So you asked about the scariest shift I've had at the warehouse. Okay, I'm Kishore, I run the evening dispatch team, and this is the one I still think about.

Shreya takes a phone call near loading bay three. Next minute she's white as chalk, one hand on the rack, knees kind of wobbling. Some of the lads assumed she was furious, because she'd been arguing with a driver earlier.

I didn't know. Could be anger, could be she was going to faint, could be bad news. So I just asked, "Are you hurt? Do you need to sit?" She shook her head, then sat on a pallet anyway. I got water, asked if she wanted anyone called.

Turned out her father had been taken to hospital. Shock, not temper. I called our supervisor to cover her line and booked her a cab. The feelings could wait; getting her safely off the floor couldn't.

qa.q: Where did Shreya take the phone call?
qa.a: She took the phone call near loading bay three.

qa.q: Why did Kishore ask about Shreya's safety before anything else, and what was Kishore feeling?
qa.a: Kishore felt uncertain and concerned, because her paleness and wobbling knees could mean anger, faintness or bad news, so Kishore checked she was not hurt or about to fall before guessing her feelings.

qa.q: How could the other workers handle a moment like this next time?
qa.a: They could stop assuming it is anger, ask a simple question about whether the person is hurt or needs to sit, and help get them somewhere safe.

qa.q: What was it like for Shreya when some of the lads thought she was furious?
qa.a: She had just heard frightening news about her father, so being read as angry would have left her more alone at a moment of shock.

grounding: It shows a young adult seeing a colleague go pale and shaky and putting safety and health ahead of reading the emotion.

passage:
I'm Yusuf, and I work the grill next to Akash on weekends. Here's what I saw on Saturday night, for whatever it's worth.

The dinner rush was at its worst. Akash dropped a plate of kebabs, and a few minutes later his face had gone pasty and there was sweat on his lip. His hands shook while he plated.

The head chef shouted, "Nerves, Akash? Toughen up!" Maybe it was nerves. The kitchen was also boiling, and I'd not seen him eat all shift.

I pulled him into the cold store and asked, "Dizzy? Want to sit?" He sat on a crate and said he felt light-headed. Someone brought sweet tea and a roti. After ten minutes his colour came back.

Later he said, "Maybe the heat, maybe the dropped plate. I don't know." I still don't know either. I just knew it wasn't the moment to call it nerves.

qa.q: What did Akash drop during the dinner rush?
qa.a: He dropped a plate of kebabs.

qa.q: How can you tell Akash was unsure about his own feelings, and what did he most likely feel?
qa.a: He said "Maybe the heat, maybe the dropped plate. I don't know," which suggests he felt shaken and light-headed, possibly embarrassed about the plate, though the heat and not eating could explain it just as well.

qa.q: What went wrong in the head chef's response, and what could fix it?
qa.a: The head chef labelled it nerves without asking; a quick check on whether Akash was dizzy, plus water or food and a seat, would have come first.

qa.q: What might Akash have felt if the head chef's "toughen up" had been the only response?
qa.a: Akash might have felt ashamed and kept working while light-headed, which could have made him more unwell in a hot kitchen.

Mentoring notes, Thursday. Written by Madhav, team lead.

Sat in on Jasleen's renewal call with the logistics client. The client opened by criticising our last report for five minutes. Jasleen kept a steady, warm voice, nodded on camera, smiled when she thanked them for the detail, then walked them through the fix. It was a good call; the client ended by booking the next review.

After we disconnected she rubbed her cheeks and said, "My face hurts from being pleasant." She laughed, but it was the fourth call like this this week.

What I did: asked how she was actually doing. She admitted she'd been swallowing irritation all week and going home flat. We agreed she'll take ten minutes between difficult calls, and that "let me check and come back to you" is always allowed. I'll check in with her again on Monday.

qa.q: How many calls like this had Jasleen had this week?
qa.a: It was the fourth call like this this week.

qa.q: What does Jasleen rubbing her cheeks and saying her face hurts suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she was tired and had been holding back irritation behind a pleasant face; it could also simply be relief that a hard call went well.

qa.q: How could Madhav keep supporting Jasleen after this call?
qa.a: Madhav could keep the Monday check-in, protect the ten-minute breaks, and remind her that saying she needs to check and come back is fine.

qa.q: How might the client have experienced Jasleen's warm, steady manner?
qa.a: The client probably felt heard rather than argued with, which may be why they booked the next review.

Wednesday, late.

Big pitch today. Vidya said on the way in, "Whatever happens, keep your face calm. They watch us more than the slides."

Then slide twelve was the old version, with last year's figures. My stomach dropped. I could feel heat climbing my neck. But I'd decided in the lift that I'd stay composed on purpose, so I kept my hands open on the table, slowed my voice and said, "Let me give you the current figure instead," and just said it from memory.

Vidya caught my eye and gave the smallest nod.

It worked. They asked good questions, not about the mistake.

On the bus home I let it all out in a long voice note to Pema about how rattled I was. I think that's the deal: I can wear calm for an hour, as long as I take it off afterwards somewhere safe.

Tenzin

qa.a: Slide twelve was the old version with last year's figures.

qa.a: The stress would pile up with nowhere to go, and the useful skill could turn into hiding feelings all the time.

Monday. Chaitanya's email lands at 9:40: "Great, the launch moved again. Love it." Madhuri reads it three times. She was the one who asked the client for the extra week. Her jaw tightens. She types a sharp reply about "doing my job," then saves it as a draft and closes the laptop.

Wednesday. On the team call she unmutes. "Chaitanya, quick one. Was Monday's email about my request? I couldn't tell if it was sarcastic." He blinks, then laughs. "Half sarcastic, at the client, who keeps changing their mind. The extra week actually saves me. Sorry, I should have written that."

The following Monday. A new email: "Sure, that'll be easy." Madhuri doesn't brood. She pings him: "Easy-easy or ironic-easy?" He replies, "Ironic, but doable 🙂." She deletes the old draft.

qa.a: Chaitanya's email lands at 9:40.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when she first read the email, and what other reading was possible?
qa.a: She felt stung and defensive, reading it as sarcasm aimed at her request, shown by her tightening jaw and sharp draft; it could equally have been a joke about the client, which it turned out to be.

qa.q: Which choice prevented a conflict, and why?
qa.a: Saving the sharp reply as a draft and asking Chaitanya directly on Wednesday prevented a fight, because it checked his intent instead of assuming it.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt if Madhuri had sent the sharp reply?
qa.a: He would probably have been surprised and hurt, since he meant the sarcasm at the client and the extra week actually helped him.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional unsure whether a work email is literal or sarcastic and checking intent to avoid a needless conflict.

Sit, Shalini, this one's about that email you're glaring at.

When I was about your age, my manager, a very dry man named Kurian, sent back my first proposal with one line: "Feel free to burn the whole draft."

I was insulted. I spent that evening writing a resignation letter in my head. I thought, he's calling my work rubbish in the rudest way possible.

Next morning my senior, a patient woman in accounts, said, "Ojas, you don't know what he meant. Go and ask." So I did, voice shaking. "Sir, did you mean the draft was bad?"

Kurian looked puzzled. "The client changed the brief last night. I meant literally start again. The draft was fine for the old brief."

I nearly quit over a sentence that was just an instruction. So before you reply to that email, ask what they meant.

The train was slowing for the tunnel when Madhav's phone buzzed. His manager, Francis: "Nice work on the deck. Really bold choices."

The client meeting was at eleven, forty minutes away, and the signal bar was already flickering.

Bold. Was that praise? Or the polite way Francis said "too much"? Madhav remembered him once calling a messy chart "adventurous" with a straight face. His thumb hovered over the file. He could redo the colour scheme on the train, strip the big photos, play it safe.

Instead, before the bars vanished, he typed: "Quick check: bold good, or bold tone-it-down? Happy to adjust before 11."

The train went dark. He sat with the question for six long minutes.

At the next station the reply arrived: "Good bold. Keep it. The client asked for something that stands out." Madhav breathed out and closed the laptop.

qa.a: The client meeting was at eleven.

qa.q: How can you tell Madhav was anxious about Francis's message?
qa.a: His thumb hovered over the file and he considered redoing the deck, and the six minutes felt long; he was anxious that "bold" might be polite criticism, though it could equally be real praise.

qa.q: What did Madhav do that a wise person would copy?
qa.a: Instead of redesigning based on a guess, he sent a short question to check whether "bold" was praise or a hint, and waited for the answer.

qa.a: Madhav would still have had time to adjust before eleven, so asking would have helped either way.

passage:
The ward sister, Ishita, pinned the new rota to the board during handover. "Payal, you're on Saturday nights now; we're short. That's fine, right?"

Every nurse in the station turned. Payal smiled, nodded and said, "Yes, sister, of course."

Ishita moved on, relieved.

But Payal's pen was pressing hard enough to tear the chart she was holding. That Saturday she had promised to take her grandmother to a family function; she'd said so weeks ago.

At the end of the shift she found Ishita alone in the medicine room. "Sister, can I say something about this morning? I smiled because I didn't want to argue in front of everyone. Actually, Saturday is hard for me."

Ishita put the tray down. "I took your smile as a yes. I'm glad you told me." They looked at the rota together and Payal swapped to Sunday.

qa.a: She found Ishita alone in the medicine room.

Hi Arnab,

Thank you for having me over for dinner with your parents on Sunday. The food was wonderful and I mean that.

There's one thing I want to say, gently, because of your message afterwards: "Glad you and Dad got along so well!"

When your father said that "design is not a real job," I smiled and kept eating. Where I grew up, you do not contradict an older person at their own table; you smile and let it pass. So I did. But I wasn't agreeing. I was quite hurt, and I went quiet for the rest of the meal.

I'm not asking you to say anything to him. I just didn't want you to think my smile meant I was fine with it. Next time something like that happens, I may say something small and polite back.

See you at work on Monday,
Kamal

Okay, so you want to know why I went quiet at the engagement? I'm Sonali, and this is embarrassing, but here goes.

Arohi's aunt stands up with the mic and says, "Sonali will give the speech at the wedding! She's the best friend!" Everyone claps. Arohi looks at me, delighted. And I smile. Big smile, hands together, nodding. In my family you don't make a scene at a function; you smile and sort it out later.

Inside, I'm panicking. I freeze in front of crowds.

Arohi hugged me after and said, "I knew you'd love it!" That was the part that stung, because my smile had told her something false.

So next morning I called her. I said, "I smiled because I didn't want to spoil the moment. I'm honestly scared of speeches. Could I write it and have your cousin read it?" She went quiet, then said, "I wish you'd told me. Yes, of course."

qa.a: Arohi's aunt stood up with the mic and announced it.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling behind the big smile, and why did she smile anyway?
qa.a: She was panicking because she freezes in front of crowds, but she smiled because her family does not make a scene at a function; the smile could easily pass for delight.

qa.q: How did Sonali clear up the misunderstanding, and what else could she try?
qa.a: She called Arohi the next morning and explained plainly; she could also ask for a quiet word at the event itself next time, before the plan spreads.

qa.a: Arohi reads it as happy agreement and says "I knew you'd love it"; after the call she realises it was politeness and wishes Sonali had told her.

passage:
The panchayat office in the small town smelled of damp files and filter coffee. Jomon, two years into his first job as a clerk, was reading out the list of households due for new water connections.

"Next, Kizhakkambalam ward, forty-two houses." Someone at the back said, "That's the Vadakkekara number." Jomon checked. They were right.

He laughed, a short, high laugh, and couldn't seem to stop. A few people laughed with him. The ward member's face stayed flat. Thomas chettan, the senior clerk, leaned back and watched.

Jomon felt his ears burn. He pressed his palm flat on the register and breathed.

"Sorry, my mistake. Vadakkekara is forty-two. Kizhakkambalam is thirty-seven. I'll correct the printed copy today." Then he read the next line.

After the meeting Thomas chettan passed his desk and tapped it twice. "That second part. Good."

qa.a: He said Kizhakkambalam is thirty-seven.

passage:
Rain streaked the windows of the small architecture office in Lisbon. Aiko, a junior designer, was presenting the kitchen plans to the client, Zeynep, over coffee.

"And the island is ninety long," Aiko said. Zeynep frowned. "Ninety centimetres? That's a stool."

Aiko looked down. She had dropped a digit: the sheet said ninety where it should say one hundred and ninety. A giggle escaped her. Then another. "Sorry, haha, sorry, it's, haha."

Zeynep put her cup down. "Is the number right or not?"

The giggling had stopped being charming. Aiko felt it. She pressed her feet into the floor and said, "No. It's wrong. The island is one metre ninety. I'll send a corrected sheet by this afternoon."

Zeynep's shoulders dropped. "Okay. Show me the rest."

Walking back to her desk, Aiko wrote on a sticky note: Say it. Fix it. Next slide.

qa.q: How long was the kitchen island really?
qa.a: The island is one metre ninety.

qa.q: How can you tell Aiko's giggling came from embarrassment and not amusement?
qa.a: It started the moment she saw her mistake and kept slipping out with "sorry, haha"; she was embarrassed and perhaps hoping to soften the moment, though it didn't help.

qa.q: What did Aiko do that fixed the moment?
qa.a: She stopped laughing, admitted the number was wrong, gave the correct size and said when the corrected sheet would come.

qa.q: How did Zeynep feel while Aiko kept giggling, and after the correction?
qa.a: Zeynep seemed frustrated and unsure whether the plans could be trusted; after the plain correction her shoulders dropped and she was ready to go on.

grounding: It shows a young professional laughing from embarrassment after a mistake and settling the room by owning the error briefly and moving on.

The college hall was noisy with the alumni reunion, old batchmates slapping backs and comparing grey hairs. Then the lights dimmed for the tribute to Joseph sir, the hostel warden, who had died last year.

His photo came up on the screen: the famous cardigan, the whistle.

Suraj glanced at Pradeep, his old roommate. Pradeep was smiling, wide, the way he used to when Joseph sir caught them sneaking in late. But tears were running down into his collar.

He leaned over and said quietly, "Good tears or hard ones?"

Pradeep laughed and wiped his face. "Both, da. He'd have hated this slideshow."

Suraj put an arm on the back of Pradeep's chair, and they watched the rest of the photos together, sometimes laughing, sometimes silent.

passage:
Honestly, the best moment of my year was at an airport. I'm Kishore; Dilnaz and I have been friends since school, and I'd gone with her mother to pick her up. She'd been working abroad for three years.

The doors slide open, and there she is with two giant suitcases, and she's grinning so wide, and at the same time she's crying, really crying. Her mother starts crying too, and laughing.

I stood there with the trolley like an idiot. My head was going: is something wrong? Did something happen on the flight? Should I step back and give them space?

So I just asked her, over her mother's shoulder, "Want me to take the bags and give you a minute?"

Dilnaz said, "Stay. I'm fine. It's just everything at once. I'm happy, and I'm sad I missed so much."

Then she pulled me into the hug too.

qa.q: How long had Dilnaz been working abroad?
qa.a: She had been working abroad for three years.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling as she grinned and cried at the airport?
qa.a: She felt happy to be home and sad about everything she had missed, all at once, as she said herself.

qa.q: What helped Kishore handle the moment well?
qa.a: Instead of guessing, Kishore made a simple offer, "Want me to take the bags and give you a minute?", and let Dilnaz say what she needed.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz's mother have been feeling as she cried and laughed too?
qa.a: She was probably overjoyed to have her daughter home after three years, with some sadness for the time apart mixed in.

grounding: It shows a young adult reading a friend who cries and smiles at once at a reunion and simply asking and sharing the moment.
